meta.title: Who really said "I pay low wages. I can take advantage of that. We're going to be successful, but the basis is a very low-wage, low-benefit model of employment"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: No. The earliest print we can find is a 2005 Wired listicle, thirteen years after Walton died, with no source. It is not in his memoir.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'I pay low wages. I can take advantage of that. We're going to be successful, but the basis is a very low-wage, low-benefit model of employment'?
meta.ogDescription: Unsourced — first printed in 2005, thirteen years after Sam Walton died, and not in his own book.

answer.label: Unsourced — first printed thirteen years after he died
answer.sourceLine: Nobody has produced a source. The earliest appearance we could document is Adam L. Penenberg’s “Why Google Is Like Wal-Mart” in Wired, 21 April 2005 ↗ — a comic side-by-side listicle that files the sentence under “Quote the company most regrets” and credits it to Walton without saying where it came from. Walton died on 5 April 1992, and the line is not in the memoir he published that year.

source.heading: Where it actually comes from

docMeta.dd: None — the line is simply signed “Sam Walton”

source.excerpt:
Quote the company most regrets:
• Wal-Mart: “I pay low wages. I can take advantage of that. We’re going to be successful, but the basis is a very low-wage, low-benefit model of employment.” — Sam Walton
• Google: “Evil is whatever Sergey says is evil.” — Google CEO Eric Schmidt
trail: Wikiquote’s Sam Walton page ↗ carries this sentence as the only quotation it records from him, and gives its provenance as “Attributed in” the Wired article — not as anything Walton wrote or was recorded saying.

We read that article in full ↗. It is a humour piece by Adam L. Penenberg, published 21 April 2005, and the sentence appears in a list headed “Quote the company most regrets”, credited to Walton with no citation.

We searched the complete text of Walton’s memoir, Sam Walton: Made in America (Doubleday, June 1992), in the Bantam printing whose own front matter states that it “contains the complete text of the original hardcover edition” and that “not one word has been omitted”. The copy catalogued at the Internet Archive ↗ is lending-restricted and cannot be searched from its catalogue page; the text we read is the Archive’s separately held full-text scan of that same printing, item made-in-america-sam-walton, so the search can be repeated. The sentence is not in it. Neither is the phrase “pay low wages”, nor “take advantage of that”, nor “low-benefit”.
Wikipedia ↗ gives Walton’s death as 5 April 1992, which puts the first documented printing thirteen years after he could have been asked about it.

The register is the tell. “A very low-wage, low-benefit model of employment” is the vocabulary of a labour economist describing a firm from outside, not of a retailer describing his own shop — and it is nothing like the voice of the memoir, where Walton writes “In the beginning, I was so chintzy I really didn’t pay my employees very well.” That is an observation about style, not evidence, and we have not treated it as evidence.
source.excerptNote: The earliest printing we found, in full context: a joke listicle comparing Google to Wal-Mart, running the two companies’ most regretted quotations side by side. No source is given for the Walton line, and the article does not claim to have one.

author.name: Sam Walton
author.heading: About Sam Walton
author.metaLine: 1918–1992 · American retailer, founder of Walmart and Sam’s Club
author.bio: Samuel Moore Walton (29 March 1918 – 5 April 1992) bought a Ben Franklin variety store in Newport, Arkansas in 1945 and opened the first Wal-Mart Discount City in Rogers, Arkansas in 1962; Sam’s Club followed in 1983. From 1982 to 1988 he was the richest person in the United States, and he received the Presidential Medal of Freedom. He told his own story once, in Sam Walton: Made in America (1992), written with John Huey and published weeks before his death.

misattribution.heading: Often misattributed
misattribution.intro: This is quoted as a confession — the founder of Walmart admitting the business model out loud. There is no record of him saying it.

items.why: The sentence is signed with his name wherever it appears, but no one who repeats it names a speech, interview, memo or book. Wikiquote ↗ can trace it only to a Wired article published in 2005, thirteen years after Walton died.

items.who: His memoir, Sam Walton: Made in America
items.why: It is often said to come from the 1992 memoir. We searched the book’s complete text and none of it is there — not the sentence, not “low-benefit”, not “take advantage of that”.

misattribution.truthLine: What is documented is the practice, not the quotation. Snopes ↗ rated a separate account of Walton’s minimum-wage manoeuvres Mostly True — and that fact-check never mentions this sentence.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: The quotation gets used because the underlying charge is real and documented. Snopes ↗, drawing on the labour historian Nelson Lichtenstein’s The Retail Revolution (2009), records that retail clerks were exempt from the federal minimum wage through the 1950s, so Walton could pay as little as fifty cents an hour; that when Congress nearly doubled the wage to $1.15 an hour and tightened the exemption, Walton “hated the new minimum wage, and he would simply not abide by it”; and that the unusual structure of his stores let him duck under the new sales threshold. Snopes is careful to add that the structure was already in place for other reasons, and was not concocted solely to skirt the law.
None of which means he said this. The gap between “the man did it” and “the man admitted it in these words” is exactly the gap a quotation is supposed to close, and here nothing closes it.
detailsBody: Walton was candid about the early years in his own book, in his own register: “In the beginning, I was so chintzy I really didn’t pay my employees very well.” That sentence is in the memoir and this one is not, which is worth noticing — a man who volunteered the first has no obvious need of the second.

What we could not establish: who first wrote the sentence. The Wired listicle is the earliest printing we found, but it presents the line as already-known rather than new, so something earlier may exist in a source we could not reach.
context.pull: Wikiquote can trace it only to a joke listicle published thirteen years after he died.

sourcesVerified.claim: Wired published "Why Google Is Like Wal-Mart" by Adam L. Penenberg on 21 April 2005; under the heading "Quote the company most regrets" it prints "I pay low wages. I can take advantage of that. We're going to be successful, but the basis is a very low-wage, low-benefit model of employment." credited to Sam Walton, with no source given.
Wikiquote's Sam Walton page carries this sentence as its only quotation and cites its provenance as "Attributed in Adam L. Penenberg, 'Why Google Is Like Wal-Mart', Wired, 21 April 2005".

Wikipedia states Samuel Moore Walton lived March 29, 1918 – April 5, 1992, founded Walmart in Rogers, Arkansas in 1962 and Sam's Club in 1983, and was the richest person in the United States from 1982 to 1988.

Snopes' fact-check "Sam Walton and Minimum Wage" (David Mikkelson, 8 June 2014) is rated Mostly True and concerns Walton's wage practices, quoting Nelson Lichtenstein's The Retail Revolution (2009). It presents the store-restructuring-to-evade narrative as the circulating account under assessment, and corrects it in its own voice: the structure was "already in place for other reasons; not, as suggested above, one that was concocted solely to skirt minimum wage laws". It does not mention the words "I pay low wages".

The Internet Archive catalogues "Sam Walton, made in America: my story" (Walton, Sam, 1918-1992). The copy held there is lending-restricted — it offers Borrow only — so the book's text cannot be searched from that page.

A full-text scan of the same Bantam printing of Sam Walton, Made in America, held at the Internet Archive as item "made-in-america-sam-walton", contains no occurrence of "I pay low wages", "take advantage of that" or "low-benefit". It does contain Walton writing "In the beginning, I was so chintzy I really didn't pay my employees very well.", and front matter stating the edition carries the complete text of the original hardcover with not one word omitted.
